name: Rumford bores a cannon and the caloric fluid dies
scope: The experiment that proved heat is motion, not a substance. T1: in the Munich arsenal around 1797-98, Benjamin Thompson (Count Rumford) had horses drive a deliberately BLUNT borer against a brass cannon sitting in a wooden box of water -- and after about two and a half hours the water BOILED, with no fire anywhere near it (the hook: boiling water, no flame). T2: the reigning theory said heat was 'caloric', an invisible weightless fluid squeezed out of the metal by the tool -- but a fluid supply runs dry, and Rumford's heat never did; he could keep the water boiling as long as the horses walked. T3: the control rung -- Rumford weighed the metal shavings and compared their SPECIFIC HEAT to ordinary brass; they were identical, so nothing material had been removed from or changed in the cannon. T4: his 1798 Royal Society paper, 'An Inquiry Concerning the Source of the Heat which is Excited by Friction', argued that anything an insulated body can supply WITHOUT LIMIT cannot possibly be a material substance -- therefore heat is motion. T5: the honest caveat -- caloric did NOT die that day; contemporaries shrugged, and Sadi Carnot still reasoned in caloric in 1824. The fluid theory only died once Joule put a NUMBER on the exchange rate decades later. T5b: the irony rung -- in 1804 Rumford, caloric's assassin, married Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, widow of Antoine Lavoisier, the chemist who had put caloric on his list of elements; they separated after about three years. T5c: the man himself -- a Woburn, Massachusetts Loyalist who commanded the King's American Dragoons against his own countrymen, then reinvented himself as a Bavarian count feeding the Munich poor with 'Rumford's Soup'.
source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Thompson' / 'Caloric theory' / 'History of thermodynamics' (direct fetch returns HTTP 403 to the tool, as logged in prior builds; consulted via domain-restricted search, which returned: Munich arsenal 1798, blunt steel borer, horse-powered, brass cannon, water in a wooden box boiled continuously, no apparent limit to heat produced, 'An Experimental Enquiry Concerning the Source of the Heat which is Excited by Friction'). Corroborated by Wikipedia 'Benjamin Thompson' (fetched: c.1797-98 Munich arsenal, specially blunted boring tool, water boiled in ~2.5 hours, specific-heat comparison of the shavings, 1798 paper title, 1804 marriage to Marie-Anne Lavoisier and separation after three years, King's American Dragoons, Rumford's Soup, death 1814). Caveat that contemporaries did not treat the result as decisive: J. Chem. Educ. 2019, 'Rumford's Experimental Challenge to Caloric Theory'.
framing_note: DISCOVERY + REVERSAL, and the sub-strand's opening scene. T1 keys the SCENE (blunt borer, horses, boiling water, no fire) -- never a date, never 'who discovered heat'. ACCURACY RAIL: Rumford's experiment did NOT immediately kill caloric -- historians are explicit that it was not seen as decisive at the time and caloric survived for decades; any rung that implies a single-day overthrow is wrong. Second rail: the borer was deliberately BLUNT (a sharp one cuts efficiently and makes far less heat) and the cannon was BRASS -- get both right. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (rub two palms hard together, or a coin on a tabletop, and feel the heat appear from nothing but motion). DISTRACTOR MINE: the graveyard of real wrong theories -- caloric, phlogiston, 'friction releases air trapped in the metal', 'the metal's own stored fire', 'the horses' body heat'. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'heat is motion' before asking what Rumford's endless boiling showed. Teach 'specific heat' in the T3 rung before any later rung leans on it.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank -- American Revolution Loyalists / the King's American Dragoons (keep Rumford's biography to ONE rung and key it to the heat science, not the war). COOKING bank -- if it carries historical kitchen technology, Rumford's Soup and the Rumford range may already exist there; science keeps only the caloric-killing experiment.

name: Joule's paddle wheel: the exchange rate between work and heat
scope: A brewer with a homemade thermometer nails the first law. T1: James Prescott Joule hung weights on strings that turned a brass paddle wheel inside an insulated barrel of water, let them fall, and measured the water's temperature rise -- falling weights make heat, at a fixed exchange rate (the hook: he was chasing temperature changes of a fraction of a degree). T2: the apparatus rung -- an eight-armed paddle wheel spinning between fixed vanes inside a copper cylinder, so the water could not simply swirl; every bit of the weights' fall had to be ground into friction. T3: Joule was not a professor. He ran his family's Manchester brewery, and his freakish thermometric precision came from the brewing trade, where a fraction of a degree is money -- the rung keys the BREWERY as the source of the skill. T4: the establishment rung -- the Royal Society REJECTED his paper in 1844; he had to settle for the Philosophical Magazine in 1845, and he presented the paddle-wheel result at the British Association meeting in Cambridge in June 1845 as 'On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat'. T4b: the number kept moving as his apparatus improved -- about 819 foot-pounds per BTU in 1845, refined toward 772 by 1850. The wonder is that a fixed exchange rate EXISTS, not what its digits are. T5: Oxford, 1847 -- in the audience sat Faraday, Stokes, and a 23-year-old William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin), 'intrigued but sceptical'. Thomson's public questioning turned Joule from a curiosity into the meeting's event, and the sceptic became his lifelong collaborator (the Joule-Thomson effect). T5b: the honeymoon rung, told honestly -- Joule married Amelia Grimes on 18 August 1847, and he and Thomson arranged to try measuring the temperature difference between the top and bottom of the Cascade de Sallanches waterfall; the attempt proved impractical. T5c: what drove him -- Joule wrote that the power to destroy belongs to the Creator alone, so any theory demanding the annihilation of force must be erroneous.
source: Grokipedia 'James Prescott Joule' and 'Mechanical equivalent of heat' (fetcher blocked, HTTP 403; consulted via domain-restricted search, which returned: 1845 brass eight-arm paddle wheel rotating between fixed vanes inside a water-filled copper cylinder, falling weights over pulleys, thermometers through the lid, ~772 ft-lb/BTU, Manchester family brewery background, early work on resistive heating). Corroborated by Wikipedia 'James Prescott Joule' (fetched: June 1845 Cambridge BAAS falling-weight/paddle-wheel demonstration, 819 ft-lbf/BTU estimate, paper read to the Royal Society 20 June 1844 and rejected, published Phil. Mag. 1845, 1847 Oxford BAAS attended by Stokes, Faraday and Thomson who was 'intrigued but sceptical', marriage to Amelia Grimes 18 Aug 1847 and the Cascade de Sallanches attempt that 'proved impractical', the 'power to destroy belongs to the Creator alone' quotation) and Wikipedia 'Mechanical equivalent of heat' (fetched: 778.24 ft-lbf value, Mayer's 1842 priority and 1845 number, the Thomson/Joule strategy on the priority dispute).
framing_note: DISCOVERY, with the amateur-beats-the-academy note. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT test the number -- Joule's value MOVED (819 ft-lb/BTU in 1845, ~772 by 1850), so a rung keyed to digits is both rote and wrong-prone; key the rungs to the apparatus, the rejection, the sceptic, and the idea of a fixed exchange rate. Second rail: the Sallanches waterfall attempt is documented AND documented to have failed -- never tell the popular version where he successfully measures the waterfall on his honeymoon. OPTIONAL RUNG (verify first at build time): Joule was privately tutored by John Dalton -- confirm before seeding. QUOTE RAIL: the 'power to destroy' line is documented and quotable; no other Joule quote may be invented. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (drop a weight, warm the water -- a kid can shake a jar of water and watch the thermometer creep up). DISTRACTOR MINE: caloric, 'heat squeezed out of the water by stirring', the real rival claimants (Mayer, Ludvig Colding, Helmholtz), and 'the thermometer was warmed by his hands' -- the actual objection sceptics raised. LANE BORDER: MATH owns unit arithmetic; HISTORY owns Manchester and the Industrial Revolution -- the brewery rung must be about THERMOMETRY, not industry.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank -- Industrial Revolution / Manchester manufacturing (keep the brewery rung about measurement precision). MATH bank -- unit conversion; never seed a conversion-arithmetic rung here.

name: Mayer and the bright red blood of the tropics
scope: The man who got there first and was broken for it. T2: in 1840, sailing to Java as a ship's doctor, Julius Robert von Mayer bled sick sailors and was startled that their VENOUS blood came out bright red, nearly as red as arterial blood -- in the tropical heat, the crew's bodies were burning far less oxygen (the hook: a colour, seen in a bucket on a ship's deck). T3: what he made of it -- if the body needs less fuel-burning when the surroundings are warm, then heat and work and food-energy are one quantity wearing different clothes, and the total never changes. He also noticed that storm-whipped waves are warmer than calm sea. T4: the reception rung -- Annalen der Physik, the leading physics journal, rejected his 1842 paper as insufficiently rigorous; it appeared instead in a CHEMISTRY journal, Annalen der Chemie und Pharmacie, where physicists would not look. T4b: his number for the mechanical equivalent of heat did not come from an experiment at all -- he derived it from published gas heat-capacity data, which is exactly why the experimentalists found it easy to dismiss. T5: the collapse -- after two of his children died and Joule's supporters brushed aside his claim to priority, Mayer attempted suicide by jumping from a window on 18 May 1850 and spent years confined in asylums; he came out, in his own circle's words, a broken man. T5b: the vindication -- John Tyndall championed him publicly from 1862, the Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal in 1871, and Joule himself conceded that the IDEA had been Mayer's while claiming the experimental proof as his own.
source: Wikipedia 'Julius von Mayer' (fetched: 1840 voyage to Jakarta as ship's physician, bright red venous blood and the oxidation inference, warmer storm-whipped waves, 1842 'Remarks on the Forces of Inorganic Nature' rejected by Annalen der Physik and published in Annalen der Chemie und Pharmacie, values of 365 then 425 kgf-m/kcal against a modern ~426.6, the Joule priority conflict, suicide attempt 18 May 1850 and institutionalisation, Tyndall's 1862 lecture and the 1871 Copley Medal). Corroborated by Wikipedia 'Mechanical equivalent of heat' (fetched: Mayer's 1848 letter to the Academie des Sciences asserting priority; Thomson and Joule's agreed response conceding the idea but claiming the verification).
framing_note: REVERSAL + the price of being early; the sub-strand's counterweight to the Joule ladder. ACCURACY RAIL: Mayer's number came from published GAS HEAT-CAPACITY DATA, not from an experiment of his own -- never write a rung that has him measuring it in a laboratory. Second rail: he SURVIVED the 1850 fall -- no rung may imply he died then (he died in 1878). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the colour of blood in the tropics). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real rival claimants (Joule, Helmholtz, Colding, Carnot's unpublished notes) and the real wrong physiology of the day -- 'vital force', the idea that animal heat comes from a special living principle rather than ordinary oxidation. Anti-restatement: the stem describes what Mayer SAW (bright venous blood, hot climate, less fuel burned) and lets the conclusion be recalled knowledge -- never state 'energy is conserved' in the stem. LANE BORDER: ANIMAL bank owns blood, circulation and respiration as creature biology; science keeps only Mayer's inference and the conservation principle.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank -- oxygen transport / venous vs arterial blood as animal physiology. Keep this ladder's blood rung anchored to Mayer's SHIP and his inference, not to how circulation works.

name: Joseph Black and the heat that hides
scope: Why a snowdrift outlasts the thaw. T1: Joseph Black asked a Glasgow question -- when the thaw comes, why does a snowdrift take DAYS to disappear instead of melting away in minutes the way a simple warming should predict? (the hook: the stubborn drift). T2: in a 1762 experiment he showed that ice sitting in a warm room soaked up heat for many times longer than the same water needed to warm through the same range -- heat was going IN with no temperature going up. He named it LATENT heat, from the Latin latens, 'lying hidden'. T3: the kid-testable rung -- put a thermometer in a pot of boiling water and turn the burner to maximum. The reading does not budge off 100 C; every extra joule goes into ripping liquid into vapour, not into raising temperature. T3b: Black also separated out SPECIFIC heat -- equal masses of different substances need very different amounts of heat for the same rise, and water's appetite is unusually large. T4: why industry cared -- Black taught at Glasgow while James Watt was the university's instrument maker. Condensing steam DUMPS its enormous hidden heat into whatever it touches, which is why the old Newcomen engines wasted most of their coal reheating a cylinder they had just chilled; Watt's answer was the separate condenser of 1765. T5: the payoff in your own body and your own kitchen -- sweating cools you because evaporating water carries off latent heat, and a steam burn is far worse than a boiling-water burn at the SAME temperature, because the steam dumps its latent heat into your skin as it condenses.
source: Wikipedia 'Latent heat' (fetched: Black's introduction of the concept around 1750 at Glasgow, the slow-melting-snow observation, the 1762 Glasgow experiment showing ice absorbing heat over ~21 times longer, the Latin latens etymology, the sensible/latent distinction, the much larger heat of vaporisation than of fusion, and the influence on Watt's 1765 separate condenser). Corroborated against the standard thermodynamics account of evaporative cooling and steam burns.
framing_note: MECHANISM, and the most kid-replicable ladder in the sub-strand. TEACH-BEFORE-TEST: the T2 rung must introduce 'latent heat' plainly before any later rung uses the term. ACCURACY RAIL: the separate condenser was WATT'S invention -- Black taught, encouraged and lent him money, and historians dispute how directly latent-heat theory caused the design; frame it as 'Black's teaching and friendship, Watt's invention', never 'Black told Watt what to build'. Second rail: at ordinary pressure steam is not HOTTER than boiling water -- it is worse to be burned by because of the latent heat it releases on condensing; say it exactly that way. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (thermometer in the pot, burner cranked, reading refuses to move). DISTRACTOR MINE: caloric, 'the water gets hotter if you turn the burner up', 'steam is hotter than boiling water', 'ice is cold because it contains cold'. LANE BORDER: COOKING owns technique -- the cooking bank already carries a boiling-vs-simmering rung; this ladder must key BLACK'S DISCOVERY and the latent-heat principle, never recipe advice.
history_overlap: COOKING bank -- an existing ladder covers boiling vs simmering (both sit at ~100 C; the difference is agitation). Do NOT seed a rung whose answer is 'both are 100 C'; key this ladder's boiling rung to Black's LATENT-heat explanation instead. HISTORY bank -- Watt and the steam engine as Industrial Revolution narrative.

name: Carnot's perfect engine and the ceiling nobody can beat
scope: A 28-year-old soldier finds the limit of all machines. T2: in 1824 a French army engineer, Sadi Carnot, paid out of his own pocket to print 600 copies of a 118-page book asking a patriotic question -- why do British steam engines beat French ones? -- and it sold almost nothing while he lived. T3: his answer used a waterfall picture -- an engine's power comes from heat FALLING from hot to cold, the way a mill wheel takes its power from water falling through a height. So what sets the power is the temperature DROP, not the fuel and not the working substance: steam, air or alcohol all give the same ceiling. T4: the shock in one line -- the best possible efficiency is 1 minus (cold temperature over hot temperature) in absolute degrees. Between boiling water at 373 K and a room at 298 K the ceiling is about 20 percent, and the engines of Carnot's day were managing 3 to 5. No cleverness with gears, oil or materials can beat the ceiling; you can only raise the hot side or lower the cold side. T4b: the corollary that made engineers uncomfortable -- a perfectly reversible engine is the BEST engine, and a perfectly reversible engine must run infinitely slowly. Real power costs real waste. T5: the deepest irony in thermodynamics -- Carnot reasoned all of it out while BELIEVING caloric, that heat is a conserved fluid that falls through the engine without being consumed. He was wrong about what heat is and right about the limit. Private notes from 1832 show he had privately abandoned caloric and had even estimated a mechanical equivalent of heat (about 370 kg-m against a modern 427) -- unpublished. T5b: the near-loss -- Carnot died of cholera in 1832 at 36 and his brother Hippolyte had most of his effects and papers burned as a contagion precaution. The book survived only because Emile Clapeyron rewrote its argument in 1834, from which Kelvin and Clausius built the second law. T5c: the ceiling today -- car engines run around 20-30 percent, power stations chase efficiency by pushing the hot side up with superheated steam, and 'a 100 percent efficient engine' is not a hard engineering target but a physical impossibility.
source: Wikipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot' (fetched: 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire' published June 1824 at his own expense, 600 copies, 118 pages, little attention in his lifetime; the reversible cycle; his acceptance of caloric; the spring 1832 private notes with 'Heat is simply motive power, or rather motion that has changed form' and the ~370 kg-m estimate against a modern 427; death from cholera in 1832 aged 36; Hippolyte's destruction of most personal papers; Clapeyron's 1834 article and the route to Kelvin and Clausius). Wikipedia "Carnot's theorem (thermodynamics)" (fetched: eta_max = 1 - T_C/T_H, no irreversible engine beats a reversible one between the same reservoirs, independence from working substance, the 373 K / 298 K worked example giving 20.1 percent, early steam engines at 3-5 percent, modern internal combustion at roughly 20-30 percent).
framing_note: MECHANISM with an honest-caveat spine. ACCURACY RAIL: Carnot's PUBLISHED reasoning assumed caloric and still produced the right limit -- do not tidy this into 'he knew heat was motion'; the abandonment appears only in unpublished notes found later. Second rail: the burning of his papers was a cholera precaution by his brother, not suppression -- no conspiracy framing. Third rail: the efficiency formula needs ABSOLUTE temperatures; if a rung uses numbers, they must be in kelvin. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the waterfall picture -- power comes from the DROP, so a hot engine in a hot room is a waterfall with no height). DISTRACTOR MINE: perpetual motion, 'better lubrication or materials can beat the limit', caloric, 'efficiency depends on which fuel you burn', 'a bigger boiler is more efficient'. Anti-restatement: never let a stem name the temperature-ratio rule before asking what Carnot found limits an engine. LANE BORDER: HISTORY owns the Industrial Revolution story; science keeps the engine physics and Carnot's reasoning.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank -- the steam engine and the Industrial Revolution; keep every rung here anchored to Carnot's ARGUMENT, not to industrial consequences.

name: Entropy and the arrow of time
scope: The theme backbone of the sub-strand: why the world has a direction. T1: you can scramble an egg but never unscramble it; stir milk into coffee and it never un-stirs. Nothing in the laws of motion forbids the reverse -- run every collision backwards and each one is legal (the hook: what actually stops it is not a law of force but a matter of odds). T2: Rudolf Clausius coined the WORD in 1865, built from Greek roots meaning 'transformation content', and said he deliberately made it SOUND like 'energy' because the two quantities are so closely related. He closed the paper with two sentences: the energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to a maximum. T3: the teaching rung -- entropy counts how many microscopic arrangements would look identical from outside. A shuffled deck is not 'messy'; it is one of an astronomically larger family of orders than the sorted one, which is exactly why shuffling looks irreversible. T3b: Clausius's own version of the second law is homelier than the equations -- heat never passes on its own from a colder body to a warmer one without something else changing too. Your coffee cools; the room never spontaneously heats it back up. T4: Ludwig Boltzmann tied entropy to that counting with S = k log W -- the formula carved on his gravestone in Vienna, though Max Planck was the first to write it in that exact form. W counts the arrangements; k converts counting into thermodynamic units. T4b: Josef Loschmidt's objection -- if every collision is reversible, entropy should fall as readily as it rises. Boltzmann's answer was that it is a matter of overwhelming probability, plus a fact about how the universe STARTED. T5: the past hypothesis -- the arrow points forward because the early universe was in a fantastically improbable low-entropy state, and WHY it was is still an open question. The bank says so proudly. T5b: Arthur Eddington coined the phrase 'arrow of time' in his 1927 Gifford Lectures (published 1928) and ranked the second law above every other law of nature -- a theory that contradicts Maxwell's equations may survive, he said, but one that contradicts the second law has no hope. T5c: heat death -- William Thomson's 1852 paper 'On a Universal Tendency in Nature to the Dissipation of Mechanical Energy' extended the idea to everything; the honest caveat is that applying thermodynamics to an entire expanding, gravitating universe is contested (gravity clumps matter rather than smoothing it, and physicists have questioned whether entropy is even well defined for a universe that has never been at equilibrium). T5d: the local-order rung -- your freezer makes ice, lowering entropy inside, only by dumping more entropy out the back through the coils; Earth is likewise not a closed system, taking in concentrated low-entropy sunlight and radiating diffuse infrared back out.
source: Wikipedia 'Rudolf Clausius' (fetched: 1865 coining from Greek en + trope, his stated preference for ancient roots so a term means the same in all languages, his wish that it resemble 'energy', the two-sentence 1865 conclusion, and the 1854/1856 statement that heat can never pass from a colder to a warmer body without another change occurring). Wikipedia 'Second law of thermodynamics' (fetched: Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements and their equivalence; Loschmidt's paradox listed). Wikipedia 'Entropy (arrow of time)' (fetched: Boltzmann's 1877 proposal, T-symmetry of microscopic laws vs macroscopic asymmetry, the low-entropy early universe as an unexplained boundary condition, and the caution against reading entropy as simple 'disorder'). Wikipedia 'Ludwig Boltzmann' (fetched: S = k log W on the tombstone; Planck named the constant). Wikipedia 'Heat death of the universe' (fetched: Thomson 1851-52 paper title, Helmholtz and Rankine, maximum-entropy equilibrium without requiring absolute zero, and the caveats -- gravity, Smolin's objection that gravitationally bound systems grow more structured, dependence on dark energy and indefinite expansion, and Planck/Buchdahl/Tisza's doubts that entropy is definable for a never-equilibrated universe). Eddington attribution verified by search: 'The Nature of the Physical World' (1928), chapter 4, from the 1927 Gifford Lectures.
framing_note: The analytic BACKBONE of the sub-strand -- a CONCEPT/THEME ladder with a native T5 ceiling. TEACH-BEFORE-TEST is load-bearing: the T3 microstate-counting rung must sit BEFORE any rung that leans on 'entropy'. ACCURACY RAIL: entropy is NOT 'disorder' -- it is a count of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state. No rung may have 'mess', 'messiness' or 'disorder' as its answer, and the messy-bedroom analogy is banned as an answer (it may appear only as a distractor). Second rail: the first law still holds during all of this -- energy is never destroyed, only made unavailable; a rung whose answer implies energy is lost is wrong. Third rail: the heat-death rung MUST carry the open-question caveat (gravity and cosmic expansion make the universe-scale claim contested) -- MYSTERY mode, no false closure, and the past hypothesis is stated as unexplained. QUOTE RAIL: reference Eddington's 'supreme position' passage by description; do not reprint it at length. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the egg and the milk swirl -- and the follow-up that the reverse is legal, just absurdly unlikely). DISTRACTOR MINE: caloric, 'energy is being destroyed', 'the second law is only about heat engines', 'entropy means things wear out', and the real historical objections (Loschmidt's reversibility, Zermelo's recurrence). STANCE GUARD: the T5d open-system rung PRESENTS the physics of local order; it must not be written as an argument for or against anything outside physics.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank -- time, determinism and causation as seminar topics. Science keeps the PHYSICAL arrow (entropy, the past hypothesis) and must not restage a metaphysics-of-time debate.

name: Perpetual motion always fails
scope: The standing public test that nobody has ever passed. T1: in 1813 a showman named Charles Redheffer charged New Yorkers admission to see a machine that ran forever. Robert Fulton watched it wobble unevenly, said no true machine runs like that, tore off a board -- and found a catgut cord running up through the wall to an old man in an attic turning a hand crank with one hand while eating bread with the other. The crowd smashed the machine (the hook: the bread). T2: he had already been caught once. In Philadelphia in January 1813, inspector Coleman Sellers noticed the GEAR TEETH were worn on the wrong side, meaning the 'output' gear was actually driving the machine; engineer Isaiah Lukens then built a convincing fake of his own, and Redheffer tried to buy it. T3: the two flavours rung -- a machine of the FIRST kind would make energy out of nothing and breaks the first law; a machine of the SECOND kind would take heat from one reservoir, say the ocean, and turn it entirely into work with no cold sink, breaking the second law. The second kind is the sneaky one, and it is what most modern 'over-unity' claims actually are. T3b: the oldest design keeps coming back -- Bhaskara's 12th-century overbalanced wheel with mercury in its spokes, which always stops because the extra leverage on the falling side is exactly cancelled by the greater NUMBER of weights on the rising side. Leonardo da Vinci mocked the seekers of perpetual motion by name in his notebooks. T4: the biggest score -- John Keely of Philadelphia raised millions from investors including John Jacob Astor IV for an 'etheric force' motor said to run on water and air. T4b: after Keely died in November 1898, a Philadelphia Press investigation published on 19 January 1899, with University of Pennsylvania physicists Carl Hering and Arthur Goodspeed, tore up his workshop and found compressed-air tubing hidden inside walls, ceilings and solid beams, and a three-ton compressed-air sphere buried in the basement. T5: the institutional rung -- the United States Patent Office will not grant a perpetual-motion patent without a WORKING MODEL, and the UK office refuses such applications as contrary to well-established physical laws. That is a standing, permanent public bet that no such device exists, open to anyone, and never collected. T5b: how to test a claim yourself -- do not ask 'can it run forever', ask 'what goes IN?'. Every device ever examined turned out to draw on something: a hidden crank, compressed air, a battery, a temperature difference, ambient vibration. Naming the input is the whole skill.
source: Wikipedia 'Perpetual motion' (fetched: violation of the first and/or second laws; USPTO working-model requirement; UK Patent Office refusal as contrary to well-established physical laws and lacking industrial application; Bhaskara's wheel as an overbalanced wheel whose torques cancel; Robert Fludd's 1618 water screw as the first documented attempt; Leonardo's 'seekers after perpetual motion' remark; the persistence of 'over unity' claims and suppression conspiracy theories). Wikipedia 'Charles Redheffer' (fetched: 1812 Philadelphia exhibition near the Schuylkill, January 1813 inspection, Coleman Sellers and the cogs worn on the wrong side, Isaiah Lukens's decoy machine which Redheffer offered to buy, the New York rebuild, Fulton noticing the unsteady crank-driven motion, the catgut cord to an elderly man turning a hand crank while eating bread, and the crowd destroying the machine). Wikipedia 'John Ernst Worrell Keely' (fetched: 'vaporic'/'etheric'/'vibratory sympathy' claims, the Keely Motor Company founded 1872 with $5 million capital, John Jacob Astor IV and Clara Jessup Bloomfield Moore as backers, the 1884 Sandy Hook 'vaporic gun' demonstration and Lieutenant Zalinski's pneumatic diagnosis, Keely's death 18 November 1898, the Philadelphia Press investigation of 19 January 1899 with Carl Hering and Arthur Goodspeed, and the discovery of hidden compressed-air tubing, a three-ton basement sphere and a concealed water motor).
framing_note: The sub-strand's SKEPTICISM flagship -- the ladder that trains the kid to demand the input. ACCURACY RAIL: Redheffer was exposed TWICE in two cities by two different people -- Sellers' worn cog teeth in Philadelphia and Fulton's catgut cord in New York. Keep them on SEPARATE rungs; fusing them is the likeliest error. Second rail: Keely was exposed AFTER his death, by a newspaper investigation with university physicists, not caught mid-demonstration. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the old man in the attic eating bread). DISTRACTOR MINE: real failed designs, which is a deep seam -- the overbalanced wheel, Fludd's water screw, capillary and self-filling-flask machines, magnet ramps, the 'zero point energy' tap -- plus the real conspiracy framing ('suppressed by the oil companies'), which a rung may NAME as a claim people make without endorsing it. STANCE GUARD (this is why vision is mandated): the ladder must hold two things at once -- test every claim, including expert-endorsed ones, AND recognise that the patent-office rule is an honest standing test rather than a cover-up. Do not let the skeptical voice slide into free-energy conspiracy, and do not let the institutional voice slide into 'the authorities have settled it, stop asking'. The T5b rung is the resolution: ask what goes in.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank -- Robert Fulton and the steamboat; keep Fulton here purely as the man who found the cord. No other sister-bank overlap.

name: Maxwell's demon and the price of one bit
scope: A thought experiment that took 145 years and an actual measurement to close. T3: on 11 December 1867, in a letter to his friend Peter Guthrie Tait, James Clerk Maxwell imagined a 'finite being' stationed at a trapdoor between two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and slow ones the other -- sorting hot from cold for free, apparently smashing the second law (the hook: a doorman who breaks physics). T3b: Maxwell never called it a demon; William Thomson pinned that name on it in Nature on 9 April 1874, meaning a Greek daemon, an agent working behind the scenes, not an evil spirit. T4: the corrected-misconception rung -- Maxwell was not claiming the second law could be broken. He was demonstrating that it is STATISTICAL: true because we deal in bulk numbers of molecules, not because any individual molecule is forbidden to move the 'wrong' way. It is usually taught as a paradox and was meant as an explanation. T4b: Leo Szilard's 1929 single-molecule engine sharpened it -- the demon has to MEASURE which side the molecule is on, and Szilard argued the measurement itself must carry a thermodynamic price. T5: Rolf Landauer, 1961, moved the price to a different place -- measuring can in principle be free, but ERASING cannot. Wiping one bit of information must dump at least kT ln 2 of heat into the surroundings, about 3 x 10^-21 joules at room temperature. Charles Bennett showed in 1982 that this closes the loophole: the demon's notebook fills up, and clearing it costs precisely what the sorting gained. T5b: the experimental rung -- in 2012 Antoine Berut and colleagues (Lyon, Augsburg and Kaiserslautern) trapped a single colloidal bead in a double-well and measured the heat released as one bit was erased. It matched Landauer's limit. A 19th-century thought experiment was finally closed by a measurement. T5c: why it is not only philosophy -- Landauer's limit is a hard floor on the energy cost of computing, and it is the reason information is treated as physical. Honest caveat: real chips run orders of magnitude above the limit, so it is not today's bottleneck.
source: Wikipedia "Maxwell's demon" (fetched: the 11 December 1867 letter to Tait describing a 'finite being'; Maxwell's avoidance of 'demon'; Thomson's use of the word in Nature on 9 April 1874 in the Greek daemon sense; Szilard 1929 on the energy cost of acquiring information; Landauer 1961 on the cost of erasure; Bennett 1982 showing erasure closes the loophole; the 2012 experimental measurement with Eric Lutz and colleagues). Grokipedia "Landauer's principle" and Wikipedia "Landauer's principle" (Grokipedia fetch blocked, consulted via domain-restricted search: Q = kT ln 2 as the minimum dissipated heat for erasing one bit; the 2012 Nature paper by Berut et al. from ENS Lyon, Augsburg and Kaiserslautern using a single colloidal particle in a time-dependent double-well potential; further confirmations from 2014 onward in classical and quantum settings).
framing_note: MYSTERY that resolves into MECHANISM -- the century-long exorcism IS the wonder. TEACH-BEFORE-TEST: the T4 'the second law is statistical' rung must precede anything that leans on it, and 'bit' must be introduced before the Landauer rungs. ACCURACY RAIL: Maxwell neither named it a demon nor believed the law was breakable -- Kelvin coined the name in 1874, in the Greek daemon sense. Second rail: Landauer's limit applies to ERASING information, not to measuring or to computing as such; reversible computation can in principle dodge it, and real processors sit far above the limit. Say both. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (deleting a file has a minimum, unavoidable heat bill -- information is physical). DISTRACTOR MINE: the historically live wrong answers, which are excellent here -- 'the demon gets tired', 'friction in the trapdoor', and especially Leon Brillouin's real 1951 proposal that the demon needs LIGHT to see the molecules and pays there (respectable, nearly right, and not the modern resolution). Never a joke option. LANE BORDER: the AI bank owns data-centre energy and computing policy; science keeps the physical floor.
history_overlap: AI bank -- energy cost of computation / data centres. Keep the T5c rung on the PHYSICS floor and hand any policy framing to the AI bank.

name: Brownian motion: how pollen made atoms real
scope: Eighty years from a jiggle to a count. T1: in 1827 the Scottish botanist Robert Brown put grains of Clarkia pulchella pollen under his microscope and saw tiny particles jittering ceaselessly, never settling, never tiring (the hook: a dance with no dancer). T2: the control rung, and the heart of the ladder -- Brown's first idea was that he was seeing LIFE, so he went and tried to kill his own explanation. He repeated the observation with ground glass, rock and metal dust, soot, and particles from wood fossilised for millions of years. Every one of them jiggled too. T3: two corrections in one rung's worth of care -- it is not the pollen GRAINS that dance but far smaller particles released from inside them, and Brown was not the first to see the effect: Jan Ingenhousz had reported the same restless motion in charcoal dust in 1785. Brown's contribution was the control and the generality. T3b: for eighty years nobody could say WHAT was doing the jostling, and meanwhile whether atoms were real objects or merely convenient bookkeeping was a live fight -- Ernst Mach demanded to be shown one, and Wilhelm Ostwald's 'energetics' tried to run chemistry without them. T4: Einstein's 1905 paper turned the jiggle into a PREDICTION with a number in it -- the particle's average squared displacement should grow in proportion to elapsed TIME (not to time squared, as a steadily pushed object would), and the constant of proportionality is tied to the number of molecules in a mole. The invisible became countable. T4b: Jean Perrin, 1908-09, did the work -- uniform gamboge resin spheres, positions plotted at fixed intervals under the microscope, Avogadro's number extracted, and independent methods agreeing with each other. Nobel Prize 1926, awarded for work on the discontinuous structure of matter. T5: the cruel timing -- Ludwig Boltzmann, who had spent a career defending atoms and had fought editors who would not let him call them anything but convenient constructs, hanged himself at Duino near Trieste on 5 September 1906, one to two years before Perrin's numbers ended the argument. T5b: the reach of it -- the same random-walk mathematics describes how a smell crosses a room, how ink spreads in water, and it was later borrowed wholesale by finance and by every diffusion model since.
source: Wikipedia 'Brownian motion' (fetched: Robert Brown 1827, Clarkia pulchella, particles WITHIN the pollen grains, his ruling out of biological origin using inorganic matter such as glass and rock dust, Einstein's 1905 model of bombardment by individual water molecules and the link between the displacement distribution and the diffusion equation, Perrin's 1908 verification, his Nobel Prize in 1926 'for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter', and the significance for the contested reality of atoms). Wikipedia 'Ludwig Boltzmann' (fetched: the long dispute with a journal editor who would not permit atoms and molecules to be called anything but convenient theoretical constructs; suicide by hanging at Duino near Trieste on 5 September 1906; Perrin's 1908-09 colloid studies confirming the Avogadro and Boltzmann constants 'a couple of years after Boltzmann's death'). Ingenhousz's 1785 charcoal-dust priority is recorded in the same Wikipedia article's history section.
framing_note: The sub-strand's flagship for the SELF-TEST virtue: Brown attacked his own favourite hypothesis and killed it, which is the whole method in one rung. ACCURACY RAILS, three of them, and they are the usual failure points: (a) it was particles released from INSIDE the pollen grains, not the grains themselves; (b) Brown was NOT the first observer -- Ingenhousz 1785 -- so no rung may key 'who first saw it'; (c) Einstein did not see or photograph atoms, he predicted a measurable statistical signature that Perrin then measured. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (fossil dust jiggles too -- so it is not alive). DISTRACTOR MINE: the genuinely live rivals of the period -- a vital force in living matter, convection currents in the water, evaporation at the surface, electrical attraction, and the energeticist position that atoms were only bookkeeping. All were held by serious people, which is exactly the point. Anti-restatement: never let a stem mention molecules colliding before asking what the jiggling turned out to be. LANE BORDER: ANIMAL and plant biology own pollen as reproduction; science owns the microscope moment and the atomic inference. PHILOSOPHY owns realism versus instrumentalism as a seminar move -- here Mach's challenge appears only as WORKING PRACTICE: what would count as showing you one?
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank -- scientific realism vs instrumentalism (Mach, Ostwald). Keep the T3b rung concrete: what Mach DEMANDED and what Perrin DELIVERED, not the epistemology seminar.

name: Defining a temperature and finding its floor
scope: How humans agreed what 'hot' means, and where the bottom is. T1: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit's zero was not a guess. It was the coldest thing he could reproduce on demand in 1724 -- a slush of ice, water and ammonium chloride, which settles at the same temperature every single time you mix it (the hook: a zero you can rebuild in a bucket). T2: Anders Celsius published his scale in 1742 UPSIDE DOWN -- 0 was the boiling point and 100 was freezing. It was flipped to the modern orientation within about a year, and exactly who deserves the credit is disputed (Jean-Pierre Christin and Carl Linnaeus both produced the modern version in 1743, with Stromer and Ekstrom also named). T2b: Celsius's real care shows elsewhere -- he specified mean barometric pressure at sea level for his boiling point, because he already knew boiling moves with pressure. T3: Fahrenheit's lasting achievement was not the numbers but the instruments -- mercury-in-glass thermometers consistent enough that two different observers in two different cities could compare readings for the first time and mean the same thing. T3b: why a scale wants an ABSOLUTE zero -- cool a gas and its pressure falls in a straight line, and every gas's line, extrapolated, hits zero pressure at the same point. William Thomson proposed the absolute scale in 1848; the floor sits at -273.15 C. T4: the correction rung -- absolute zero is not 'all motion stops'. Quantum zero-point energy remains; it is the point of minimum possible energy, where nothing further can be extracted. T4b: the third law says you cannot get there in a finite number of steps, because every cooling method removes a FRACTION of what is left rather than a fixed amount -- the last step never finishes. This is not an engineering problem awaiting a better fridge. T5: how close we have come anyway -- Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied helium in 1908; laser cooling and evaporative magnetic cooling have taken atom clouds into the picokelvins, with 38 picokelvin reached in a 2021 drop-tower experiment using matter-wave lensing of a rubidium condensate. For scale, the coldest known natural place, the Boomerang Nebula, sits at about 1 kelvin -- billions of times warmer. T5b: in 2019 the world stopped defining temperature by a substance at all -- the kelvin is now fixed by assigning an exact value to the Boltzmann constant, so a temperature is defined by a constant of nature rather than by a jar of water.
source: Wikipedia 'Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit' (fetched: first successful mercury-in-glass thermometers, experiments from 1713, the 1724 account's fixed points -- a frigorific mixture of ice, water and ammonium chloride or sea salt at zero, water freezing near 30, body temperature near 90 -- the later redefinition giving an exact 180-degree interval and 32/212, and his reputation for thermometers consistent enough for different observers to compare readings). Wikipedia 'Celsius' (fetched: the 1742 scale with 0 as boiling and 100 as freezing, calibration at mean barometric pressure at sea level, Christin's 1743 inversion and Linnaeus's independent reversal the same year with the credit disputed among Christin, Linnaeus, Elvius/Stromer and Ekstrom, and the 1948 renaming from centigrade). Wikipedia 'Absolute zero' (fetched: 0 K = -273.15 C = -459.67 F, Kelvin's 1848 proposal arriving at about -273 C, the third law's finite-steps impossibility, 38 picokelvin in 2021 by matter-wave lensing of rubidium condensates, the Boomerang Nebula at about 1 K as the coldest known natural environment, and residual zero-point energy from the uncertainty principle).
framing_note: A METHOD ladder -- how a measurement becomes trustworthy enough that strangers can compare notes. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) Celsius's original scale really was inverted, and the credit for flipping it is DISPUTED -- say 'flipped within about a year; exactly by whom is argued', never crown a single person; (b) absolute zero is NOT 'no motion' -- zero-point energy remains, and a rung whose answer is 'all movement stops' is wrong; (c) the 38 pK record is a laboratory matter-wave result, not a bulk material at that temperature -- phrase it as an atom cloud. ANTI-ROTE RAIL, and this is the big risk on this topic: NO rung may have a bare conversion, a bare fixed-point number, or a definition as its answer. The answers must be the CHOICES people made and the REASONS -- a reproducible brine, a scale printed upside down, a constant of nature replacing a jar of water. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the scale on your wall was published backwards). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real historical fixed points -- body temperature, the freezing of mercury, deepest local winter, water's triple point -- plus the standard wrong beliefs ('absolute zero means no motion', 'a good enough freezer could reach it', 'Celsius named it centigrade'). LANE BORDER: MATH owns conversion arithmetic entirely.

name: Dewar's flask and the three roads heat travels
scope: A thermos does not know what you put in it. T1: a vacuum flask has no idea whether your drink is hot or cold -- it simply slows the traffic in BOTH directions, which is why the same object keeps soup hot and lemonade cold (the hook: the thing that 'knows' does not know anything). T2: James Dewar built the first one in 1892 as laboratory equipment for holding liquefied gases -- a chamber inside another chamber with the air pumped out from between them. The picnic flask is a spin-off of cryogenics; it was never designed for soup. T2b: the mechanism, one road at a time -- pumping out the gap removes the molecules that would have carried heat by conduction and by convection, and silvering the facing surfaces reflects thermal radiation back where it came from. Three roads, all blocked. T3: the leak that is left -- most of the remaining heat flow goes through the NECK and the stopper, where there is no vacuum, which is why the lid matters more than the walls and why an open flask empties its heat fast. T3b: the kid-testable misconception -- a metal railing and a wooden bench in the same room are at the SAME temperature, yet the metal feels colder. Your skin does not measure temperature; it measures heat FLOW, and metal draws heat out of your hand far faster than wood does. T4: the business ending -- Dewar never patented it. Two German glassblowers, Reinhold Burger and Albert Aschenbrenner, built a rugged version for everyday use, patented it in 1904, and ran a public competition to name it; a resident of Munich won with 'Thermos', from the Greek therme, heat. Dewar sued and LOST.
source: Wikipedia 'Vacuum flask' (fetched: Dewar's 1892 brass chamber within a chamber with the intervening space evacuated, made for cryogenic work; his refusal to patent, which allowed others to develop it; Reinhold Burger and Albert Aschenbrenner's rugged 1904 domestic design; their claim to the product rights and the Thermos trademark; Dewar losing the court case; genericisation of the mark in the US in 1963; and the mechanism -- partial vacuum suppressing conduction and convection, silvering minimising radiation, and most residual heat transfer occurring at the neck and opening where there is no vacuum). The 1904 public naming contest won by a Munich resident, from Greek therme, corroborated across Thermos company heritage pages and Grokipedia 'Thermos LLC' surfaced by domain-restricted search.
framing_note: MECHANISM, with a hard commercial caveat. ACCURACY RAIL: do not turn the patent story into a theft narrative -- Dewar chose not to patent, the Germans built a genuinely different rugged consumer product, and Dewar lost in court. Say all three plainly. Second rail: the vacuum does not 'keep cold in'; cold is not a thing that moves. Every rung must speak in terms of heat FLOWING, never of cold flowing -- this is the ladder that fixes that misconception, so it must not commit it. Dinner-test payoff: T3b (walk around the house touching metal and wood in the same room). DISTRACTOR MINE: 'the vacuum keeps the cold in', 'silver is a good insulator' (it is a superb conductor -- it is there as a MIRROR), 'the flask has a heater', plus real adjacent insulation physics that is genuinely right for other cases -- double glazing, aerogel, the loft in a down jacket, fur trapping still air. LANE BORDER: the COOKING bank already owns conduction/convection/radiation applied to cooking appliances; this ladder must stay on DEWAR and the flask, never on how to cook with each mode.
history_overlap: COOKING bank -- an existing heat-transfer ladder applies conduction, convection and radiation to cooking appliances (grilling, roasting). Do NOT seed a generic 'name the three modes' rung; key every rung here to the FLASK, the neck leak, or the metal-versus-wood touch test.

name: Plasma: the fourth state, and the one nobody teaches
scope: You were taught three states, and the universe mostly runs on a fourth. T1: ask a child to name the states of matter and you get solid, liquid, gas. Stars are made of none of them; nor is a lightning bolt, nor the glow inside a neon sign (the hook: the most common state of ordinary matter is the one that never made it onto the classroom poster). T2: what makes it a genuinely different state and not just a very hot gas -- heat a gas enough and electrons are torn off their atoms, so the stuff is full of free charges. It CONDUCTS electricity and it obeys magnets, neither of which a gas does; and its particles act collectively at long range rather than in one-on-one collisions. T3: the naming rungs -- William Crookes proposed a fourth state he called 'radiant matter' in 1879 after watching the glow in evacuated discharge tubes; Irving Langmuir supplied the name 'plasma' in 1928, and his colleague Mott-Smith recalled that the way the ionised gas carried particles along reminded Langmuir of blood plasma carrying corpuscles. T3b: where a kid can actually see it -- lightning, a neon or fluorescent tube, the hottest part of a gas flame, the Sun, and the aurora, where particles from the solar wind are funnelled down Earth's magnetic field lines. T4: the honest open rung -- because plasma answers to magnetic fields, fusion reactors try to hold it inside magnetic bottles; and because it is a fluid full of instabilities, it keeps squirming out. Controlled fusion power is not a solved problem, and the bank says so.
source: Wikipedia 'Plasma (physics)' (fetched: Crookes's 1879 fourth-state proposal from low-pressure electrical discharge work; Langmuir's 1928 coining and Mott-Smith's recollection of the blood-plasma analogy; the statement that 99.9% of all ORDINARY matter in the universe is plasma; the three distinctions from gas -- long-range collective interactions rather than short-range binary collisions, very high electrical conductivity versus gases as excellent insulators, and multiple independently acting species; and everyday examples including lightning, auroras, neon signs, sufficiently hot flames and the Sun).
framing_note: The 'you were taught three and there are four' hook, which is the whole appeal. ACCURACY RAIL, and it is the one that will get missed: state the abundance claim PRECISELY -- plasma is the most common state of ORDINARY (baryonic) matter. Dark matter and dark energy make up most of the universe's content and are not plasma. No rung may say '99% of the universe is plasma' without the ordinary-matter qualifier. Second rail: Crookes deserves credit for the fourth-state INTUITION, not for a correct mechanism -- he thought his radiant matter was a stream of charged molecules, and cathode rays turned out to be electrons; frame him as right in instinct, wrong in detail. Dinner-test payoff: T3b (look at a neon sign, a gas flame or the aurora and know you are looking at the universe's default state). DISTRACTOR MINE: the other real states, which are excellent adjacent-but-wrong answers -- Bose-Einstein condensate, supercritical fluid, degenerate matter -- plus 'plasma is just a very hot gas' and 'the fourth state is fire'. LANE BORDER: GEOGRAPHY owns the aurora as a place to go and see; science keeps the ionisation mechanism and the magnetic funnelling.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY bank -- the aurora as a place-anchored phenomenon (northern-lights destinations). Key the aurora rung to IONISATION and magnetic field lines, not to where to view it.

name: The Mpemba effect: a schoolboy's question nobody has closed
scope: A mini gem in MYSTERY mode. T3: in 1963, in a cookery class in Tanzania, a schoolboy named Erasto Mpemba put his ice-cream mix into the freezer while it was still HOT, because the freezer was filling up and he wanted a space -- and his froze before the classmates' cooled mix. His teacher told him he had confused himself (the hook: the boy was told he was wrong, and he was not confused). T4: when the physicist Denis Osborne visited the school, Mpemba asked him the question anyway. Osborne, openly sceptical, went away and TESTED it rather than dismissing it, and published the result jointly with Mpemba in 1969 -- the schoolboy's name is on the paper. Aristotle, Francis Bacon and Descartes had all reported something similar in earlier centuries and been forgotten. T5: the honest status rung -- there is still no settled mechanism, and the effect may not even be a real general phenomenon. Candidates include evaporation reducing the mass, dissolved gases, convection currents, differences in supercooling, and frost layers acting as insulation. Careful experiments by Burridge and Linden in 2016 found no reproducible effect at all, while other groups continue to report one. This is a live argument and the bank refuses to declare a winner.
source: Wikipedia 'Mpemba effect' (fetched: Mpemba's 1963 observation in a cookery class in Tanzania, his question to Denis Osborne about 35 C versus 100 C water, Osborne's initial scepticism followed by experimental confirmation and the joint 1969 publication, the earlier reports by Aristotle, Bacon and Descartes, the proposed mechanisms -- supercooling, hydrogen bonding, dissolved gases and convection, frost insulation, mineral precipitation from boiling -- the 2016 Burridge and Linden conclusion of no evidence for meaningful observations of the effect, later reports finding it in controlled Peltier-cell experiments, and the summary that reproducibility, definition and cause all remain contested).
framing_note: MYSTERY mode, three rungs, no more -- brevity is the point. ACCURACY RAIL, absolute: do NOT assert that the effect is real. Reproducibility, and even how to define it, are contested; Burridge and Linden found nothing, other groups report something. Any rung that treats it as established fact fails. Second rail, and it follows: every distractor here is a PROPOSED mechanism, and none of them may be quietly designated the true answer -- the correct answer on the T5 rung is that no one yet knows. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- a kid can literally run this with two ice-cube trays, and the right lesson is the grown-up one: a careful run may show nothing at all, and that is a real result. This is the ladder that teaches 'test it yourself' with an honest possibility of a null. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real proposed mechanisms above, plus the real dismissals ('he mismeasured', 'the hot tray melted the frost and made better thermal contact' -- which is itself one of the live hypotheses). LANE BORDER: COOKING owns freezing and ice-cream technique; science keeps Mpemba, Osborne and the open question.
history_overlap: COOKING bank -- freezing technique / ice cream. Keep every rung here on the ARGUMENT (a boy's question, a sceptic who tested it, an unresolved mechanism), never on how to freeze food.
